T10-0.1x shows poor stability: 1.62 to 1.14 mmol g-1 (29.5% loss), barely better than uncoated. The divergence despite identical TMC:TAPA mass ratios reveals local TMC concentration critically affects coating defect formation. At moderate concentration (2 wt.%), interfacial polymerization proceeds at controlled rates allowing uniform network formation. The exothermic reaction and HCl evolution are manageable as heat dissipates through solution while HCl escapes gradually without disrupting coating.27,28 At 10 wt.% (10x concentrated, 1/10 volume), the same total TMC reacts much faster. 24 a ) b ) Rapid polymerization generates intense localized heating (estimated 20-30°C rise based on adiabatic calculations) combined with vigorous HCl evolution that physically disrupts forming polymer. This creates structural defects (micropores, cracks, incomplete crosslinking) providing amine leaching pathways during thermal cycling. This parallels PA membrane literature showing excessive monomer concentration increases defect density. 27,28 The fact that T10-0.1x shows similar kinetics to T2-0.5x (18.2 min vs 17.8 min) despite poor stability supports the defect hypothesis: CO bypasses coating through defect pathways 2 (maintaining reasonable kinetics) while defects permit amine evaporation (poor stability). This asymmetric selectivity occurs because CO diffusion needs only small pathways while amine 2 retention requires complete encapsulation. T2-0.5x's moderate initial capacity (1.33 mmol g-1 vs 1.61 mmol g-1 for T1-4x) reflects some amine loss during coating due to reduced solution volume (7.5 mL vs 60 mL), but this is compensated by exceptional stability and superior kinetics. Figure 17b shows T2-0.5x reaches 95% capacity in 17.8 min (1.3x slower than T1-1x), compared to T1-4x at 18.8 min. T2-0.5x's kinetic advantage over T1-4x despite similar stability results from coating localized at pore mouths without extensive oligomerization within pores. At 2 wt.% with 0.5x volume (7.5 mL), polymerization is rapid and confined to external surfaces. Limited solution volume restricts TMC penetration time, minimizing oligomer formation within pores. The amine phase retains low viscosity, allowing rapid CO diffusion once gas traverses the 2 thin external coating. T2-0.5x shows less biphasic uptake than T1-4x, with gradual transition between phases, suggesting thinner/more permeable coating allowing sustained uptake. T1-4x's abrupt transition indicates distinct layers (external coating and viscous oligomer-enriched region) creating pronounced diffusion barrier. T2-0.5x emerges as optimal due to 98.5% retention (27-fold improvement), 1.3-fold kinetic penalty, requiring only 7.5 g solvent per 0.1 g sorbent. It balances sufficient solution volume for uniform particle wetting and complete surface coverage, moderate TMC concentration enabling controlled polymerization without defects, minimal volume limiting oligomer formation and maintaining favorable kinetics, and practical, scalable synthesis. Figure 18 shows the comparison of the optimized PA-coated sorbent with uncoated sorbent in 10 adsorption-desorption cycles under dry conditions. The optimized PA-coated sorbent exhibited negligible CO capacity loss over 10 cycles, while base uncoated sorbent had >30% 2 capacity loss. This further indicates the great potential of PA-coated sorbent for long-term, stable DAC. 25 Figure 18.
